sources.title: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.supported_claim: A governance model can define roles, responsibilities, policy, oversight, risk priorities, and review cycles.
sources.limitations: The CSF governs cybersecurity risk, not marketing automation. Any use in the article must be labeled as an operating-governance analogy, not a NIST marketing standard.

supported_claims: Governance can use explicit roles, responsibilities, policy, oversight, risk prioritization, and recurring review.
unsupported_claims: NIST requires a specific marketing-automation process, or the proposed governance framework guarantees security, compliance, data quality, or operational performance.
drafting_constraints: Label NIST CSF 2.0 as a governance analogy rather than a marketing-automation standard.
Do not claim security, privacy, or legal compliance from workflow governance alone.
Use synthetic workflow examples with no private client or system data.
Require organization-specific access, privacy, and change-control review.

sources.title: About Performance Planner
sources.supported_claim: Google Ads provides forecast scenarios for eligible campaigns to assess how budget or campaign-setting changes may affect selected metrics.
sources.limitations: Google Ads only; forecasts are modeled estimates, eligibility and feature support can change, and forecasts do not establish causal incrementality.

supported_claims: Google Ads offers modeled planning scenarios for eligible campaigns and selected conversion goals.
unsupported_claims: A forecast proves incrementality, a marginal signal guarantees better returns, or the same platform behavior applies across Google, Meta, TikTok, or other channels.
drafting_constraints: Treat forecasts and marginal signals as decision inputs, not causal proof.
Keep the framework platform-neutral except where the reviewed Google documentation is explicitly identified.
Do not include current feature coverage, eligibility thresholds, or numeric benchmarks unless rechecked at publication time.
Require controlled change windows and post-change observation before further reallocation.

sources.title: Manage your business — Marketing and sales
sources.supported_claim: A marketing plan can identify multiple channels, document costs, and use consistent measurement to review the plan.
sources.limitations: General planning guidance; it does not prove that channel diversification will improve acquisition results or prescribe an optimal channel mix.

supported_claims: A marketing plan can document channels, costs, and a consistent review process.
unsupported_claims: Using more channels necessarily lowers acquisition cost, improves growth, or produces a safer or more profitable mix.
drafting_constraints: Frame platform concentration as a business-risk diagnosis and planning inference, not a guaranteed diversification benefit.
Do not prescribe a universal channel count or allocation.
Use synthetic scenarios only and distinguish measurement signals from proof.
Require a staged test and operational-capacity check before adding a channel.

sources.title: Plan your business — Break-even point
sources.supported_claim: Contribution margin relates selling price and variable cost and can support a break-even estimate.
sources.limitations: Foundational small-business guidance, not ecommerce-specific accounting advice; cost classification and model inputs require business-specific review.

supported_claims: Contribution margin can be represented from selling price and variable cost inputs and used in break-even reasoning.
unsupported_claims: Any universal ecommerce cost classification, profit threshold, benchmark, or claim that the model guarantees a profitable marketing decision.
drafting_constraints: Use a clearly synthetic worksheet and label every assumed input.
Present the model as management guidance, not accounting, tax, or financial advice.
Do not state benchmarks, results, or universal cost inclusions.
Require finance or accounting review before a business adopts the model.

sources.title: CAN-SPAM Act: A Compliance Guide for Business
sources.supported_claim: U.S. commercial email is subject to sender-identification, truthful-message, address, opt-out, and compliance-monitoring requirements described by the FTC.
sources.limitations: U.S. federal guidance only; it is not legal advice and does not replace jurisdiction-specific review. Penalty amounts and legal requirements must be rechecked before publication.

sources.title: Email sender guidelines
sources.supported_claim: Gmail documents authentication, subscription, unsubscribe, formatting, and monitoring requirements for mail sent to personal Gmail accounts.
sources.limitations: Gmail-specific and time-sensitive; sender-volume thresholds, enforcement, and technical requirements must be rechecked before publication.

supported_claims: Retention email operations should account for truthful sender/message information, unsubscribe handling, authentication, recipient expectations, and ongoing monitoring.
unsupported_claims: Universal legal compliance, deliverability guarantees, fixed optimal cadence, or any claim that a retention workflow guarantees repeat purchases.
drafting_constraints: Do not provide legal advice; tell readers to verify rules for every applicable jurisdiction.
Distinguish commercial, subscription, and transactional messages without declaring a reader's legal classification.
Treat Gmail requirements as provider-specific and time-sensitive.
Avoid deliverability, engagement, revenue, and retention benchmarks.
